title: Lecture 5. Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns
summary: This lecture introduces essential design patterns for object creation and structural composition in software engineering. Students will learn the Gang of Four patterns including Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Adapter, Composite, and Decorator. The lecture emphasizes practical application, pattern selection criteria, and real-world implementation strategies within object-oriented systems.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and motivation behind design patterns in software construction
Apply creational patterns (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory) to solve object creation problems
Apply structural patterns (Adapter, Composite, Decorator) to organize class and object composition
Evaluate and select appropriate patterns based on design requirements and trade-offs
Implement design patterns using object-oriented principles including inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation
Recognize design patterns in real-world software systems and frameworks

sections.title: Introduction to Design Patterns
learningGoals: Understand what design patterns are and why they matter
Recognize the historical context and Gang of Four contribution
Identify the three main categories of design patterns

subsections.title: What Are Design Patterns?
keyPoints: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design
Not finished code, but templates for solving problems in various contexts
Capture expert knowledge and best practices accumulated over decades
Provide a shared vocabulary for developers to communicate design decisions
Balance between flexibility, reusability, and complexity
examples: Analogy: Architectural patterns in building construction (arches, columns)
Recipe vs. actual meal: pattern vs. implementation

subsections.title: Gang of Four and Pattern Categories
keyPoints: Design Patterns book (1994) by Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides
23 classic patterns organized into three categories
Creational patterns: object creation mechanisms
Structural patterns: object and class composition
Behavioral patterns: object interaction and responsibility (next lecture)
Patterns work together and complement each other
examples: Java Collections Framework uses multiple patterns
GUI frameworks heavily rely on structural and behavioral patterns
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Taxonomy diagram showing the three pattern categories with examples

exercises: Identify potential design problems in a given code snippet that could benefit from patterns
Match common software design problems to appropriate pattern categories

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Singleton
learningGoals: Understand when and why to use Singleton pattern
Implement thread-safe Singleton in object-oriented languages
Recognize the trade-offs and criticisms of Singleton

subsections.title: Singleton Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide global access point
Use when exactly one object is needed to coordinate actions across system
Private constructor prevents external instantiation
Static method provides controlled access to the single instance
Lazy vs. eager initialization strategies
examples: Configuration manager for application settings
Logger instance shared across application
Database connection pool manager
Device driver for hardware resource
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Singleton structure with private constructor and getInstance() method

subsections.title: Singleton Implementation and Concerns
keyPoints: Thread-safety issues in multi-threaded environments
Double-checked locking pattern for lazy initialization
Enum-based Singleton in Java (best practice)
Criticisms: global state, testing difficulties, hidden dependencies
Violates Single Responsibility Principle (manages lifecycle + business logic)
Consider alternatives: dependency injection, factory patterns
examples: Thread-safe Singleton implementation in Java and Python
Problems with Singleton in unit testing (mocking difficulties)
Refactoring Singleton to dependency-injected service
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code comparison showing naive vs. thread-safe Singleton implementations

exercises: Implement a thread-safe Singleton for a configuration manager
Identify problems in a given Singleton implementation
Refactor code using Singleton to use dependency injection instead

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Factory Method
learningGoals: Apply Factory Method to delegate object creation to subclasses
Understand the relationship between Factory Method and polymorphism
Distinguish between Factory Method and simple factory functions

subsections.title: Factory Method Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Define interface for creating objects, let subclasses decide which class to instantiate
Defers instantiation to subclasses through inheritance
Creator class declares factory method returning product type
Concrete creators override factory method to return specific product instances
Promotes loose coupling between creator and concrete products
Follows Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification
examples: Document editor creating different document types (Text, Spreadsheet, Presentation)
GUI framework creating platform-specific UI components
Logistics system with different transport methods (Truck, Ship, Plane)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Creator-Product hierarchy with factory method

subsections.title: Factory Method in Practice
keyPoints: Template Method pattern often uses Factory Method
Parallel class hierarchies: creators and products
Can use parameters to select product variant within same factory method
Difference from static factory methods (simple factories)
When to use: when class cannot anticipate type of objects to create
Trade-off: requires subclassing, increases number of classes
examples: Java Iterator pattern (Collection.iterator() factory method)
Framework hooks for application-specific object creation
Game engine creating different enemy types based on level
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing factory method invocation and object creation flow

exercises: Design a Factory Method solution for a payment processing system with multiple payment types
Extend existing Factory Method implementation to support new product variant
Compare Factory Method vs. direct instantiation in terms of flexibility and complexity

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Abstract Factory
learningGoals: Apply Abstract Factory to create families of related objects
Understand how Abstract Factory ensures product compatibility
Distinguish Abstract Factory from Factory Method

subsections.title: Abstract Factory Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Provide interface for creating families of related/dependent objects without specifying concrete classes
Creates multiple products that are designed to work together
Abstract factory declares creation methods for each product type
Concrete factories implement methods to create specific product variants
Ensures products from same family are used together
Client code works with factories and products through abstract interfaces
examples: UI toolkit creating widgets for different platforms (Windows, macOS, Linux)
Furniture shop creating matching furniture sets (Victorian, Modern, ArtDeco)
Game creating themed environment elements (Medieval, SciFi, Fantasy)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Abstract Factory with multiple product families

subsections.title: Abstract Factory vs. Factory Method
keyPoints: Abstract Factory uses object composition, Factory Method uses inheritance
Abstract Factory creates product families, Factory Method creates single products
Abstract Factory often implemented using Factory Methods
Adding new product types requires changing all factory interfaces (limitation)
Adding new product families only requires new concrete factory (strength)
Consider when product variants must be used together consistently
examples: Cross-platform GUI framework ensuring consistent look-and-feel
Database abstraction layer with different SQL dialects and connection types
Document converter supporting multiple input/output format combinations
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison table and diagram showing Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory

exercises: Design Abstract Factory for cross-platform notification system (email, SMS, push)
Extend Abstract Factory to support new product family without modifying existing code
Identify when to use Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory in given scenarios

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Adapter
learningGoals: Apply Adapter pattern to integrate incompatible interfaces
Implement both class and object adapters
Recognize adapter usage in existing frameworks and libraries

subsections.title: Adapter Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Convert interface of class into another interface clients expect
Allows classes with incompatible interfaces to work together
Two variants: Class Adapter (inheritance) and Object Adapter (composition)
Wraps existing class with new interface without modifying original code
Promotes reusability of existing code in new contexts
Also known as Wrapper pattern
examples: Integrating third-party library with different interface than your system expects
Legacy system integration with modern applications
Power adapter analogy: US plug to European socket
Java InputStreamReader adapting InputStream to Reader interface
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing both Class Adapter and Object Adapter structures

subsections.title: Adapter Implementation Strategies
keyPoints: Object Adapter: uses composition, more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees
Class Adapter: uses multiple inheritance (where supported), more efficient
Two-way adapters allow interface to work in both directions
Adapter can add additional functionality beyond interface conversion
Trade-off: adds indirection layer, slight performance overhead
Consider when: cannot modify existing code, need to use several existing subclasses
examples: Adapting legacy Rectangle class to modern Shape interface
Database driver adapters for different DBMS vendors
Media player adapter supporting various audio formats
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code example showing Object Adapter implementation with delegation

exercises: Implement adapter to integrate third-party logging library with your application's logger interface
Design two-way adapter for bidirectional communication between incompatible systems
Identify adapters in Java Collections Framework or other standard libraries

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Composite
learningGoals: Apply Composite pattern to represent part-whole hierarchies
Implement tree structures with uniform treatment of individual and composite objects
Understand recursive composition and its applications

subsections.title: Composite Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies
Lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly
Component interface defines operations for both leaf and composite objects
Leaf represents primitive objects with no children
Composite stores child components and implements child-related operations
Recursive composition: composites can contain other composites
examples: File system: files and directories (directories contain files and other directories)
GUI components: containers and widgets (panels contain buttons, labels, other panels)
Organization hierarchy: employees and departments
Graphic drawing: shapes and groups of shapes
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Component-Leaf-Composite structure with tree visualization

subsections.title: Composite Pattern Implementation
keyPoints: Transparency vs. safety trade-off in component interface design
Transparent: child management in Component (uniform but unsafe for leaves)
Safe: child management only in Composite (safe but not uniform)
Parent references for traversing tree upward
Ordering of children may or may not matter
Caching results for performance optimization
Visitor pattern often used with Composite for operations
examples: Menu system with nested menus and menu items
Expression tree for mathematical expressions or compilers
Scene graph in 3D graphics engines
Document structure with sections, paragraphs, and text runs
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing recursive operation execution through composite tree

exercises: Implement Composite pattern for file system with size calculation operation
Design organization chart using Composite with salary calculation across hierarchy
Add new operation to existing Composite structure without modifying existing classes

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Decorator
learningGoals: Apply Decorator pattern to add responsibilities dynamically
Understand how Decorator provides flexible alternative to subclassing
Implement decorator chains for combining multiple behaviors

subsections.title: Decorator Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Attach additional responsibilities to object dynamically
Provides flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality
Decorator conforms to interface of component it decorates
Decorator contains reference to component and forwards requests to it
Can add behavior before/after forwarding request
Multiple decorators can be stacked to combine behaviors
examples: Java I/O streams: BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream
GUI components: adding scrollbars, borders to windows
Coffee shop: adding milk, sugar, whipped cream to coffee
Text formatting: adding bold, italic, underline to text
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Component-ConcreteComponent-Decorator structure

subsections.title: Decorator vs. Inheritance and Implementation
keyPoints: Decorator adds responsibilities at runtime, inheritance at compile-time
Avoids feature-laden classes high in hierarchy
More flexible than static inheritance: can mix and match decorators
Can apply multiple decorators in different orders
Drawback: many small objects, can complicate debugging
Component interface must be sufficient for all decorators
Decorator is not identical to component (identity issues)
examples: Stream processing pipeline with multiple filters
Middleware chain in web frameworks
Notification system with multiple delivery channels
Data compression and encryption layers
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Object diagram showing decorator chain with multiple decorators wrapping component

exercises: Implement decorator chain for text processing (encryption, compression, encoding)
Design notification system using decorators for different delivery methods
Compare decorator approach vs. inheritance for adding features to a class

sections.title: Pattern Selection and Application
learningGoals: Evaluate design problems to select appropriate patterns
Understand trade-offs and consequences of pattern choices
Recognize when not to use patterns (anti-patterns)

subsections.title: Criteria for Pattern Selection
keyPoints: Identify the design problem and forces at play
Consider flexibility requirements: compile-time vs. runtime
Evaluate coupling and cohesion implications
Assess complexity cost vs. flexibility benefit
Consider team familiarity and maintainability
Multiple patterns may solve same problem differently
Patterns are not always the answer: YAGNI principle
examples: Choosing between Factory Method and Abstract Factory based on product families
Adapter vs. Facade for interface simplification needs
When Singleton is actually appropriate vs. dependency injection
Decorator vs. Strategy for adding behavior
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree or flowchart for pattern selection based on requirements

subsections.title: Patterns in Real-World Systems
keyPoints: Patterns rarely appear in isolation in real systems
Patterns collaborate and complement each other
Framework design heavily relies on pattern combinations
Recognizing patterns in existing code aids understanding
Refactoring to patterns vs. designing with patterns upfront
Over-engineering risk: applying patterns unnecessarily
Pattern evolution: modern interpretations and variations
examples: Java Collections Framework: Iterator, Factory Method, Composite
Spring Framework: Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method
GUI frameworks: Composite, Decorator, Observer, Strategy
ORM frameworks: Factory, Proxy, Template Method
Refactoring example: evolving simple code to pattern-based design
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Architecture diagram showing multiple patterns working together in a framework

exercises: Analyze given codebase to identify which patterns are used and why
Select appropriate patterns for a new system design scenario with specific requirements
Refactor procedural code to incorporate appropriate design patterns
Critique over-engineered code that misuses patterns
